You can change the order of a sentence to emphasize a particular word or phrase.
There are several different ways that emphasis can be changed:
Inversion involves changing the normal order of a sentence. You can put the prepositional phrase before the verb and the verb before the subject.

Normal structure: The weasel jumped out of the box.
Inversion: Out of the box jumped the weasel.
Fronting involves moving a clause from the end of a sentence to the front.

Normal structure: I don't know who is going to pay for all of this.
Fronting: Who is going to pay for all of this, I don't know.
Clefting or Pseudo Clefting involves beginning the sentence with “It is/was” or “What”.

John spilled the coffee because he was in a rush.
It was John who spilled the coffee.
It was the coffee that John spilled.
It was because he was in a rush that John spilled the coffee.

I don't like when you talk back to me.
What I don't like is when you talk back to me.

Identifying Stress in Words with Suffixes
You can look at the end of a word (the suffix) to determine where the stress is in that particular word.
The syllable that gets the accent depends on which suffix comes at the end of the word.
If the word ends with -ic or -tion, the stressed syllable (vowel) is one syllable from the end.
If the word ends with -y or -ate, the stressed syllable is two syllables from the end.

images.text: The Nile, the longest river on the planet , has sustained life for eons. A narrow strip of land along the Nile's river banks and the delta at the mouth of the river has provided enough food to support a wealthy culture for thousands of years. In mid-June,  Akhet -- or inundation -- began. In the past farmers let their land flood, leaving behind a layer of rich black mud. At this time farmers would mend tools or go fishing. Not until October did the growing season begin.

It wasn't until  recently that the Nile river was not left to flood its bank.  In the twentieth century, the Egyptian population grew so extensively, that flood control techniques were initiated with the construction of the Aswan Dam. The dam, which was completed in 1970, allows people to control the Nile waters in a system of reservoirs. These collect surplus water and release it slowly when and where it is needed for agriculture.

River control, however, has brought new problems. Farmers must use artificial fertilizers since they are no longer able to enjoy the river's gift of rich black mud, and the Nile delta is in serious danger of soil erosion and salinity. What is happening is that the soil is slowly being lost and what is left is becoming saltier. This not an ideal situation in the slightest!
Moreover, the future of the Nile lies in question. As the population continues to increase and water becomes even more scarce, what will happen to the Nile? What will happen to those who inhabit its banks?
